newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma trial panelist struggles on death penalty.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma trial panelist struggles on death penalty.

text.p: The first lawyer questioned as a potential juror in the Oklahoma City bombing case Thursday struggled with the prospect of voting for the death penalty, saying she feared she would never sleep again if she did.
"I don't know if I would ever sleep again," the 80th prospective juror said. "To me, you become the executioner."
District Court Judge Richard Matsch was understanding, saying "your answers tell me this is something you have struggled with in your mind and probably in your soul."

The judge, prosecutors and defence attorneys have quizzed jury candidates for 14 days on a number of issues including the death penalty. Most of those quizzed so far have said they could vote to execute defendant Timothy McVeigh if he is found guilty of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.

On Thursday McVeigh looked intently at the woman, the first attorney to appear as a potential juror, leaning forward during the discussion about the death penalty. Dressed in a burgundy coloured shirt, with sleeves neatly rolled up, he wrote notes and conferred with his attorneys.

To be among the 12 jurors or six alternates, potential jurors must be able to say they can consider all alternatives during a sentencing hearing if McVeigh is convicted. If jurors are totally opposed to the death penalty or believe it is the only punishment they could vote for they would be excluded.
A jury is expected to be selected by next week and once it starts attorneys on both sides will have to restrict their performances to the courtroom.

Matsch Wednesday issued a written gag order reiterating his earlier directive that all parties in the case refrain from making statements outside the courtroom. The jury will not be sequestered and the judge wants to make sure they are not exposed to comments from lawyers outside the courtroom.

Security remained tight around the federal complex in downtown Denver that includes the courthouse as Saturday's anniversaries of the Oklahoma bombing and the 1993 siege at the Branch Davidian complex near Waco, Texas, approached.
Observances of the bombing anniversary are expected to be low key. A Catholic Church in downtown Denver will toll its bells 168 times, once for each victim of the bombing.
